model/stuck: Training should make a model give the right answer more often. But many models pick each answer at random, and a random draw has no slope for training to follow.
model/ask: Ask a model seven times eight, and it does not always give the same answer. It samples: fifty six half the time, fifty four three times in ten, and sixty four the rest. Those are its probabilities, written pi.
model/reward: A checker marks each answer: one if it is right, zero if it is wrong. That mark is the reward, R: a plain number, from outside the model.
model/theta: Training should make the right answer come up more often, and all it can change are the model's weights. Here they are three scores, one per answer, which a softmax turns into the probabilities. Numbers that training changes are called parameters, written theta.
average/nudge: The usual tool for improving a model is the gradient: nudge a parameter, and watch the result move. So slide theta zero, the score of fifty six, along this axis, and draw one answer at each setting.
average/jump: Each draw is right or wrong, so every reward sits at one or at zero, scattered by chance. Nudge theta zero a hair, and the reward does not slide: it stays put, or it jumps. A random draw has no slope.
average/avg: But average many draws at each setting, and the jumps smooth into a curve. That average is the expected reward, J. Ronald Williams made it the goal in 1992, for networks whose outputs are random.
average/J: Over many draws, each answer turns up as often as its probability, so J is each probability times its reward, added up. Here, zero point five times one, plus zeros: zero point five.
average/any: Rewards can be any numbers. Mark sixty four, the worst miss, as minus one, and J drops: zero point five minus zero point two is zero point three.
average/only: The rewards come from the checker and never move. Only the probabilities move with theta, so the gradient of J is each reward times the gradient of its probability, added up.
average/lost: But look: no probability weighs those terms any more. J was an average over draws; its gradient, written this way, is not.
trick/two: A small identity puts that probability back, and it comes from the slope of a log. On the left, pi of fifty six against theta zero: an S that climbs as the score climbs. On the right, its log, ln pi.
trick/nudge: Nudge theta zero up by zero point zero one. pi of fifty six was zero point five; now it is zero point five oh two five.
trick/dpi: It rose zero point zero zero two five for a step of zero point zero one: a slope of zero point two five, written partial pi, partial theta zero.
trick/dlog: Its log rose zero point zero zero five, twice as much: a slope of zero point five, written partial ln pi, partial theta zero.
trick/why: Why twice? A log counts growth relative to size. pi grew by half a percent of itself, and its log grew by about that fraction: zero point zero zero five.
trick/rule: That is the chain rule: the slope of ln u is one over u, so the slope of ln pi is the slope of pi, divided by pi. zero point two five over zero point five is zero point five.
trick/trick: It holds for every answer and every parameter, for slopes up or down: the gradient of pi is pi times the gradient of ln pi. This is the log trick.
trick/payoff: Put it into the gradient of J, and each term gets its probability back: pi, times R, times the gradient of ln pi. The gradient is a probability-weighted sum again, just like J.
try/p1: Try one. For one parameter, theta zero, an answer y has pi of y of zero point two, and partial pi, partial theta zero of zero point one six. What is partial ln pi, partial theta zero?
try/a1: Divide the slope of pi by pi: zero point one six over zero point two is zero point eight. The smaller the probability, the steeper its log.
